posts.title: An AI agent is software. Ship it like software.
posts.alt: Diagram of an AI agent release pipeline: version, stage, release, monitor, with rollback one step away.
posts.post:
An AI agent is software. Ship it like software.

Many teams take an agent from a working demo straight to customers, then hope it holds up.

Ordinary software practice already solves most of this:

→ Keep prompts, tool definitions and config in version control
→ Test changes in staging, away from real customers
→ Release one known version at a time
→ Monitor real behavior, and keep rollback one step away

When an agent does something strange, the first question is "which version ran?" If you can't answer that, you can't fix it.

This matters more every quarter. In McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey, about two in ten respondents say their organization has reached the scaling phase with AI agents.

How does your team track changes to its agents today?

#AIAgents #AIEngineering #Automation
posts.comment: Source: McKinsey, The State of AI 2026 → https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai
posts.artTitle:
An AI agent is software.
Ship it like software.
posts.artAlt: Illustration of a friendly robot on an assembly line passing through version, test and launch gates, with a rewind arrow back to the start.
posts.post2:
Your AI agent changed last week. Can you say exactly what changed?

If the answer is no, you have a demo, not a system.

Production AI needs the same habits as any other software:

1. Every prompt and tool change is versioned
2. Every change is tested before customers see it
3. Every release can be rolled back in one step

It sounds basic. It's also where many agent problems start: a quiet edit nobody tracked.

About two in ten respondents in McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey say their organization has reached the scaling phase with AI agents. Scaling without version control is how small mistakes become big ones.

What's your rollback plan if your agent misbehaves tomorrow?

#AIAgents #SoftwareEngineering #Automation

posts.title: Change one thing. Then measure.
posts.alt: Illustrative before-and-after bar chart comparing cost, latency and accuracy after a single change to an AI agent.

blog.title: How to Test an AI Chatbot Before It Talks to Your Customers

posts.post:
Change one thing. Then measure.

Tuning an AI agent usually means balancing three numbers: cost per task, response time and accuracy.

The common mistake is to swap the model, rewrite the prompt and add a tool in the same release. Results improve, or get worse, and nobody can say why.

A slower method gives you answers you can trust:

1. Pick one variable
2. Run it against the same test set
3. Record cost, latency and accuracy
4. Keep the change only if the numbers say so

It's boring work, but it's how teams get gains that last.

Which number do you check first when you tune an agent?

#AIAgents #Optimization #WorkflowAutomation
posts.comment: The full testing method, step by step → https://www.dijaedadula.com/how-to-test-an-ai-chatbot
posts.artAlt: Illustration of a robot turning one highlighted dial while speed, cost and accuracy gauges respond.
posts.post2:
"We improved the bot" isn't a result. "Replies got faster and cost per conversation went down" is.

When an AI agent gets better, someone should be able to say which change caused it.

That only happens if you change one thing at a time:

→ Same test set before and after
→ One variable per release: the model, the prompt or a tool
→ Cost, speed and accuracy recorded every time

Change three things at once and you'll never know what worked, or what to undo.

What was the last change you made to your AI, and how did you measure it?

#AIAgents #ContinuousImprovement #Automation

posts.title: If an agent acted, you should be able to see why.
posts.alt: Checklist of five things to log for every AI agent action: input, tool calls, output, approver, timestamp.

blog.title: What Is an AI Agent? A Plain-English Guide

posts.post:
If an agent acted, you should be able to see why.

For any agent that touches customers, money or data, log five things on every action:

✓ Input: what it was asked
✓ Tool calls: every system it touched
✓ Output: what it said or did
✓ Approver: who signed off, if anyone
✓ Timestamp: when it happened

With those five, "the AI did something weird" becomes a question you can answer in minutes, not a guessing game. Compliance reviews get easier too.

NIST's AI Risk Management Framework puts this kind of work under four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. Logging sits squarely in Measure and Manage.

What does your audit trail look like today?

#AIGovernance #AIAgents #RiskManagement

posts.title: "Training an AI" rarely means building a model from scratch.
posts.alt: Diagram of a person comparing two AI answers against guidelines, and the model learning from consistent judgments.
posts.post:
"Training an AI" rarely means building a model from scratch.

In published research, much of the human work is feedback. A person looks at two answers from a model and judges which is better, against clear guidelines. The model learns from many of those judgments.

Two papers show how far this goes:

→ 2017: Christiano et al. trained agents on human preferences while giving feedback on less than 1% of the agent's interactions.
→ 2022: In OpenAI's InstructGPT study, people preferred answers from a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained this way over answers from the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3.

The lesson is that a smaller model can win when the feedback is good. The hard part isn't the math. It's agreeing on what "a good answer" means, consistently.

How would you define a good answer in your field?

#AI #MachineLearning #HumanInTheLoop
posts.comment:
Christiano et al., 2017 → https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03741
Ouyang et al., 2022 → https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155
posts.artAlt: Illustration of a hand placing a checkmark on one of two answer cards on a scale while a robot takes notes.
posts.post2:
Bigger isn't always better. Better feedback often is.

In OpenAI's 2022 InstructGPT study, people preferred answers from a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained with human feedback over answers from the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3.

That's a model with about 100 times fewer parameters winning on what people actually wanted.

The idea builds on a 2017 paper by Christiano et al., which trained agents on human preferences with feedback on less than 1% of their interactions.

The quiet lesson for every business using AI: the quality of human judgment shapes the quality of the output.

Who in your team decides what a good answer looks like?

#AI #MachineLearning #HumanInTheLoop

posts.title: The first reply wins more deals than the best reply.
posts.alt: Diagram of a lead follow-up system: capture every lead in one place, first reply in under a minute, follow up until they decide, then a person takes over.

blog.title: How to Automate Lead Follow-Up With AI

posts.post:
The first reply wins more deals than the best reply.

When someone messages your business, they're rarely asking only you. They asked two or three others at the same time.

Harvard Business Review's research on online sales leads reached a simple conclusion: most companies don't respond nearly fast enough.

The fix isn't a bigger team. It's a system:

→ Every lead lands in one place, not five inboxes
→ The first reply goes out in under a minute, day or night
→ Follow-up keeps going until the person decides
→ The moment they reply or book, automation stops and a person takes over

Speed gets you the conversation. A person still closes it.

How long does your business take to answer a new inquiry today?

#LeadGeneration #AIAgents #SalesAutomation

posts.title: Ask what your AI costs per resolved conversation.
posts.alt: Five chatbot ROI metrics: speed to first reply, containment rate, conversion rate, cost per conversation and handoff quality.

blog.title: The 5 Chatbot ROI Metrics That Matter

posts.post:
Don't ask what your AI costs per month. Ask what it costs per resolved conversation.

Monthly fees hide the real picture. A cheap bot that resolves nothing is expensive. A pricier one that closes sales can pay for itself.

Five numbers tell you whether an AI agent is earning its keep:

1. Speed to first reply
2. Containment rate: conversations resolved without a person
3. Conversion rate
4. Cost per conversation
5. Handoff quality: does the person who takes over see the full context?

Set a baseline before launch, or you'll have nothing to compare against.

My rule: measure the AI the way you'd review a new team member, on outcomes, not activity. Message counts are activity. Closed sales and saved hours are outcomes.

Which of these five do you track today?

#AIAgents #CustomerExperience #ROI
posts.comment: The five metrics, one ROI formula and a worked example → https://www.dijaedadula.com/chatbot-roi-metrics
posts.artAlt: Illustration of a coin dropping into a chat bubble that becomes a checkmark, beside a balanced scale.
posts.post2:
A chatbot that costs little and resolves nothing is the most expensive tool you own.

Price per month is the wrong question. Value per conversation is the right one.

Before you judge any AI agent, write down five numbers from the month before launch:

1. Time to first reply
2. Share of conversations resolved without a person
3. Conversion rate
4. Cost per conversation
5. How often a handoff reaches a person with the full context

Then compare the month after. That's your ROI, not a vendor's estimate.

Which of these numbers do you already have today?

#AIAgents #ROI #BusinessAutomation

posts.title: Customers don't hate AI. They hate being trapped by it.
posts.alt: 64% of customers would prefer companies didn't use AI for customer service; their top worry is that reaching a person gets harder. Four handoff questions.

blog.title: How to Qualify Leads in Messenger Automatically

posts.post:
64% of customers would prefer companies didn't use AI for customer service.

That's from a Gartner survey of 5,728 customers. Their top worry wasn't wrong answers. It was that reaching a person would get harder.

So the answer isn't "no AI." It's AI with a clear exit.

A good handoff plan answers four questions:

→ When does the AI step aside? Complaints, refunds, big orders, or any time someone asks for a person
→ Who picks it up, and how fast?
→ Does that person see the full conversation, or start from zero?
→ How is it measured? Track handoff rate and time to a human reply

Customers don't hate AI. They hate being trapped by it.

Where does your AI hand off to a person today?

#CustomerService #AIAgents #CustomerExperience

The fastest way to make customers hate your AI: make it impossible to reach a person.

In a Gartner survey of 5,728 customers, 64% said they'd prefer companies didn't use AI for customer service. Their top concern was that it would get harder to reach a person.

A simple rule set to start with:

→ "Talk to a person" works on the first request, every time
→ Complaints, refunds and large orders go to a person automatically
→ The person sees the full conversation, so the customer never repeats themselves

Good AI handles the routine. Good handoffs protect the relationship.

Can a customer reach a person in your business in one step?

posts.title: Your AI agent is only as good as its instructions.
posts.alt: Checklist for briefing an AI agent like a new hire: role, audience, offers, tone, rules, what never to say, when to hand off.

blog.title: How to Write AI Agent Instructions for Any Business

posts.post:
Your AI agent is only as good as the instructions you give it.

Most weak chatbots aren't a model problem. They're a briefing problem. The agent was never told who it serves, what it may promise, or when to stop.

A strong instruction covers what you'd tell a new hire: the role, the audience, the offers, the tone, the rules, what it must never say, and when to pass the conversation to a person.

My rule: if you can't explain a situation clearly enough for a new staff member to handle it on day one, don't give it to the AI yet. Write it down for the person first. When the written version works for people, it's ready for the agent.

What's the one rule your AI agent keeps breaking?

#AIAgents #PromptEngineering #Automation
posts.comment: The 9-part instruction structure and five copy-ready templates → https://www.dijaedadula.com/ai-agent-instructions-template
posts.artTitle:
Brief your AI agent

posts.artAlt: Illustration of a robot on its first day at work reading an onboarding binder at a tidy desk.

Your AI isn't confused. It was never briefed.

Every rule you leave out, the AI fills in with a guess. That's where wrong prices, made-up policies and awkward replies come from.

Before you blame the model, check the instruction:

→ Does it say who the AI serves, and who it doesn't?
→ Does it list what it may promise, and what it must never say?
→ Does it name the sources of truth for prices and policies?
→ Does it say exactly when to hand the conversation to a person?

If a new hire couldn't work from it on day one, neither can your AI.

What's missing from your AI's instructions right now?

#AIAgents #PromptEngineering #CustomerService

posts.title: A chatbot answers. An agent acts. MCP is how it acts.
posts.alt: Diagram of an AI agent connected through MCP to a CRM, calendar, files and database, with a timeline: introduced November 2024, donated to the Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025.

blog.title: What Is MCP? A Plain-English Guide for Business Owners

posts.post:
A chatbot answers. An agent acts. MCP is how it acts.

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to the systems where your data lives: your CRM, calendar, files and databases.

Anthropic introduced it in November 2024. In December 2025, it was donated to the new Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, co-founded by Anthropic, Block and OpenAI. Anthropic counted more than 10,000 active public MCP servers at the time.

For a business, that means connecting AI to your tools is becoming a standard, not a custom project.

It also means new risk. An agent that can update your CRM can also update it wrongly. Start read-only, add write access one tool at a time, and log every action.

Which system would you connect to an AI agent first?

#MCP #AIAgents #Integration

posts.title: AI doesn't fix a broken process. It runs it faster.
posts.alt: Bar chart: nearly three-quarters of AI high performers redesign workflows, compared with about one-quarter of other organizations (McKinsey 2026).
posts.post:
AI doesn't fix a broken process. It runs it faster.

McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey found that nearly three-quarters of AI high performers redesign their workflows around AI. Among everyone else, it's about one in four.

The difference isn't the model. It's the order of operations.

Before building anything, I work through eight questions:

1. Objective
2. Current process
3. Bottleneck
4. System design
5. Automation
6. AI
7. Measurement
8. Optimization

Notice where the tools come in: almost last.

What process in your business would you fix before automating it?

#AIStrategy #WorkflowAutomation #AIAgents

McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey points the same way: nearly three-quarters of AI high performers redesign workflows around AI, compared with about one in four of everyone else.

posts.title: Your chatbot speaks for your business. Legally, too.
posts.alt: Moffatt v. Air Canada, February 2024: the company is responsible for its chatbot's answers. A four-step test loop: real questions, define correct, test and name failures, re-test.

blog.title: How to Test an AI Chatbot Before It Talks to Your Customers

posts.post:
Your chatbot speaks for your business. Legally, too.

In February 2024, a Canadian tribunal decided Moffatt v. Air Canada. The airline's website chatbot gave a customer wrong information about bereavement fares. Air Canada argued the chatbot was responsible for its own actions.

The tribunal disagreed. The company is responsible for all the information on its website, whether it comes from a static page or a chatbot.

The lesson for any business using AI: test it before it talks to customers.

→ Build a test set from real customer questions
→ Define what a correct answer looks like
→ Run the tests, name each failure, fix the root cause
→ Re-test after every change

If you can't test it, don't ship it.

How do you check your AI's answers before customers see them?

#AIGovernance #Chatbots #RiskManagement
posts.comment:
Case summary: American Bar Association, Business Law Today (Feb 2024) → https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2024-february/bc-tribunal-confirms-companies-remain-liable-information-provided-ai-chatbot/

Your chatbot speaks

"The chatbot said it" is not a defense.

In Moffatt v. Air Canada (February 2024), a Canadian tribunal held the airline responsible for wrong fare information its website chatbot gave a customer. The argument that the chatbot was responsible for its own actions didn't hold.

Three practical rules follow for any business:

→ Your AI answers only from approved sources: prices, policies, terms
→ Anything uncertain goes to a person, not a guess
→ Every change to the AI is tested before it goes live

Your chatbot is part of your website, and your website is your word.

Who reviews what your AI tells customers?

posts.title: Clients don't buy a chatbot. They buy what changes after it's live.
posts.alt: Illustrative package ladder for automation services: fix one bottleneck, build the full system, then a monthly optimization retainer.

blog.title: How to Package and Price AI Automation Services

posts.post:
Clients don't buy a chatbot. They buy what changes after it's live.

That's why pricing automation work by the hour hurts both sides. The client watches the clock. You get paid less for working faster.

A better structure:

→ Sell the outcome: faster replies, more bookings, fewer manual hours
→ Offer a package ladder, not one price
→ Run the numbers with the client: what does the problem cost today?
→ Add a monthly retainer for monitoring and improvement
→ Protect your scope in writing

My rule: never quote on the first call. Use it to understand the problem and the numbers behind it, then come back with a written proposal tied to those numbers. A quote given before you understand the problem is a guess, and clients can tell.

How do you price your automation work today?

#Freelancing #Consulting #AIAutomation

If you charge by the hour for automation, you get paid less every time you get better.

Clients don't want hours. They want answered inquiries, booked calls and time back.

A simple shift:

1. Find the cost of the problem first: missed leads, slow replies, manual hours
2. Price against that value, not your time
3. Offer three levels, so the client chooses the scope, not whether to buy
4. Add monthly optimization, because AI systems need tuning

My rule: never quote on the first call. Understand the problem and the numbers first, then send a written proposal tied to them.

posts.title: Get clients without living on social media.
posts.alt: Seven-part client system for consultants, coaches and freelancers, with instant answers and follow-up highlighted as where AI helps most.

posts.post:
You don't need to live on social media to get clients. You need a system that keeps working when you log off.

For consultants, coaches and freelancers, it has seven parts:

1. Be specific about who you help and what changes for them
2. Publish content that gets found, not just seen
3. Give people a useful first step
4. Answer every inquiry instantly
5. Make booking effortless
6. Follow up until they decide
7. Turn clients into proof

AI helps most with 4 and 6: instant answers and patient follow-up. The rest is clarity and consistency.

An hour a day is enough when the system does the remembering.

Which of the seven is the weakest link in yours?

posts.title: Assist first. Automate second.
posts.alt: Two modes compared: assist, where the AI drafts and a person approves, and automate, where the AI handles it and a person reviews exceptions. Move parts to automate once they have earned it.

blog.title: What Is an AI Agent? A Plain-English Guide

posts.post:
Assist first. Automate second.

Full automation is tempting: let the AI handle every conversation and walk away. Sometimes that works. But you give up control, and you learn less.

Assistive AI works differently. It drafts the reply, flags intent and suggests the next step. A person approves, edits or takes over.

Three things happen when teams start this way:

→ Answers become consistent across staff, VAs and freelancers
→ The team sees exactly where the AI is reliable and where it isn't
→ You learn what's safe to automate fully, based on evidence

Then you automate the parts that have earned it.

Where would assistive AI help your team most?

#AIAgents #HumanInTheLoop #CustomerExperience
posts.comment: When you need an agent, and when a simpler setup is enough → https://www.dijaedadula.com/what-is-an-ai-agent

posts.post2:
The best first AI project isn't full automation. It's a better assistant for your team.

Let the AI draft replies, flag buying intent and suggest next steps. Let your people approve, edit or take over.

You get three things fast:

→ Consistent answers across your whole team
→ A clear view of where the AI is reliable
→ Evidence for what's safe to automate fully

Then automate the parts that have earned it, not the parts that sounded easy in a demo.

Is your team using AI as an assistant yet, or still deciding?

#AIAgents #HumanInTheLoop #FutureOfWork
